Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
Value Name: Very Expensive (>10% of household income for basic service)
revision_notes: The original africanews 2016 article only reports a 10% tariff cut and does not itself establish an affordability level. Cross-checked against AREI (2023 continental platform report), which gives an average electricity cost of US$0.21/kWh in 2022; the World Bank Sustainable Electrification Project ICR, which notes tariffs based on March 2016 rates (over US cents 18-30/kWh range) with only press reports (unverified) of reductions in 2023; and an April 2025 African Business interview with Djibouti's energy minister describing Djibouti as having 'one of the highest electricity tariffs in Africa'. Against Djibouti's GNI per capita of roughly US$3,400, a basic ~200 kWh/month household bill (~US$500/year at 2022 average cost) equates to around 15% of GNI, above the >10% threshold. Score 1 (Very Expensive) confirmed.
revised_comments: Djibouti has among the highest residential electricity tariffs in Africa, with an average cost of around US$0.21 per kWh in 2022, reflecting heavy reliance on imported and diesel-based thermal generation. A basic monthly consumption of around 200 kWh therefore costs in the order of 15% of GNI per capita, well above the 10% threshold for affordable service, and government officials continue to describe national tariffs as among the highest on the continent despite periodic reductions.

Definition: Percentage of national population with access to electricity (grid or off-grid). This is the primary indicator of energy infrastructure availability for ICT. Based on World Bank/IEA Tracking SDG7 data, national statistical offices, or Afrobarometer surveys.
revision_notes: World Bank Open Data (SDG7 Tracking / ESMAP electrification dataset) confirms a national electricity access rate of 65.2% for Djibouti in 2023, matching the figure and sources originally cited. This falls within the 50-74% band. Score 3 confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: Around 65.2% of Djibouti's population had access to electricity in 2023, according to World Bank/ESMAP SDG7 tracking data, placing the country in the 50-74% access band.

Definition: The gap between urban and rural electricity access rates. A smaller gap indicates more equitable energy distribution, critical for ensuring ICT infrastructure can serve the whole population, not just cities.
revision_notes: The original source (a 2025 World Bank results page) reports only the national access rate (65%) and does not itself state an urban-rural gap; the cited '>60pp' figure is unsupported by that source. World Bank Open Data (indicators EG.ELC.ACCS.UR.ZS and EG.ELC.ACCS.RU.ZS, SDG7 Tracking/ESMAP), confirmed on the primary data.worldbank.org page for the urban series and corroborated by a secondary aggregator citing the same World Bank series for the rural figure, shows urban electricity access of 74.6% and rural access of 37.0% in 2023 - a gap of approximately 38 percentage points. This falls in the 21-40pp band rather than >60pp. Score revised from 1 to 3.
revised_comments: Electricity access is markedly higher in Djibouti's urban areas (74.6% in 2023) than in rural areas (37.0%), a gap of around 38 percentage points, according to World Bank/ESMAP SDG7 tracking data. This reflects the concentration of grid infrastructure around Djibouti City, though rural access has improved gradually through World Bank-supported grid-extension and off-grid electrification projects.

Definition: The number and activity level of technology hubs, incubators, accelerators, and co-working spaces focused on technology and innovation. These provide physical infrastructure and support for tech entrepreneurship and skills development.
revision_notes: The original AfriLabs page was evidently checked around 2019 and recorded as showing no hubs. The current AfriLabs directory lists two active Djibouti members: CTID (Centre de Technologie, d'Innovation pour le Developpement), the country's first incubator, established in 2017 and still running regular events as of 2024 (Djibouti FinTech Forum, Code4Youth training cohorts); and Startup Factory Djibouti / Startup Djibouti, a government-backed accelerator under the Ministry of Digital Economy and Innovation running active IGNITE incubation and BUILD acceleration programmes with grant funding, evidenced by activity into 2024. This amounts to two identified, reasonably active hubs, which fits the '1-2 hubs' band rather than 'None identified'. Score revised from 1 to 2.
revised_comments: Djibouti has two identifiable technology and innovation hubs: CTID (Centre de Technologie, d'Innovation pour le Developpement), the country's first incubator, established in 2017 and still organising regular entrepreneurship events and training cohorts; and Startup Djibouti (formerly branded Startup Factory Djibouti), a government-backed accelerator under the Ministry of Digital Economy and Innovation offering incubation and acceleration programmes with grant funding. Both remain active as of 2024, though the ecosystem is still small.
